title: Oxtail Stew
subtitle: Slow-braised oxtail in a rich, dark gravy
excerpt: Oxtail sections slow-braised for three to four hours in red wine, beef stock, and aromatics until the meat falls from the bone and the braising liquid reduces to a glossy, collagen-rich sauce. One of the richest braises in British cooking.

recipe.sourceNotes: Oxtail is among the most flavourful cuts of beef, containing large amounts of collagen in the joints that dissolve to gelatin during long, slow cooking and give the braising liquid a viscous, lip-coating quality that no other cut can replicate. Once dismissed as offal-adjacent peasant food, oxtail has enjoyed a sustained rehabilitation in British restaurant cooking from the 1990s onwards, partly through the influence of chefs like Fergus Henderson who championed nose-to-tail eating. The dish has parallels across cuisines — rabo de toro in Spain, coda alla vaccinara in Rome, oxtail soup in the Caribbean — and reflects the universal wisdom of using every part of the animal. The key technique is to brown the oxtail deeply before braising, which develops the Maillard compounds that give the stew its dark, savoury depth.

recipeTools.notes: A large, heavy casserole with a tight-fitting lid.

content.text: Brown the oxtail in a very hot, dry pan in batches: there is enough fat in the meat to brown without added oil. Skim the braising liquid during cooking, or make the stew the day before and refrigerate overnight. The fat solidifies on the surface and lifts off cleanly, leaving a better sauce.

items.preparation: cut into sections; ask the butcher to do this

content.text: Season the oxtail sections generously with salt and pepper. Heat a large casserole over high heat. Brown the oxtail in batches, turning every 2 minutes, until deeply coloured on all sides. Remove and set aside. The oxtail will release its own fat as it colours.

Pour away most of the excess fat, leaving 2 tablespoons in the pan. Add the onion, carrot, and celery and cook over medium heat for 8 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and tomato purée and cook for 2 minutes.

Pour in the red wine and let it bubble for 3 minutes. Return the oxtail to the pan, add the stock, thyme, and bay leaves. The liquid should come about two-thirds up the oxtail. Bring to a simmer, cover tightly, and cook over the lowest possible heat for 3.5 to 4 hours. Turn the oxtail once halfway through.

The oxtail is ready when the meat is falling off the bone and the sauce is thick and glossy. Skim any fat from the surface. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Scatter with parsley and serve with mashed potato, polenta, or crusty bread.
